tutorial.intro: This tutorial uses an invented practice case in the same tools as the study. Nothing here is scored, and every name, fact, score and description in it is made up. Your progress is saved, so you can pause and come back on any device with your private link.

lessons.title: The source and its candidates
steps: This practice case uses two small invented ontologies. The source concept comes from one; the five candidates come from the other.
Candidates are listed in the system’s initial order, with a matching score. The initial position is a suggestion, not an answer: your rank is whatever you decide.
Inspect a different candidate, then go back to one you inspected before. Inspecting a candidate never ranks it.

requirements.label: Inspect a candidate other than the first
Return to a candidate you inspected before

lessons.title: Context: parents, children and missing information
steps: Open Hierarchy. The source and the candidate each have their own browser.
Search the source ontology for “crate” and choose a result. Then open one of its parents and one of its children.
The source concept has two parents (multiple inheritance). Some candidates have no definition; the page says so instead of leaving a gap, and missing information is not a contradiction.
Use “Return to …” to come back to the compared entity.

lessons.title: Where each statement comes from
steps: Statements marked “Original” come from the ontology. Generated text sits in a dashed “Generated” frame and cites the records it rests on.
Open a citation under a generated description to see the exact original record.
In a card, use “Show original axiom” to see a restriction in its original form.
Open Evidence and select a feature (“Show in graph”), or use “Show where it appears” from a citation, to find the same record in the list.

requirements.label: Find a record in the evidence list

lessons.title: The optional evidence graph
steps: The evidence graph shows the same items as the evidence list. The list is a complete alternative if you prefer it.
Select a line in the graph to read what it means, or select an item in the list. Try zoom or “Fit all”.
With the graph or list open, add or move a candidate in your practice answer: the view stays where it was.

requirements.label: Inspect a line in the graph or an item in the list
Change your practice answer with the graph or list open

lessons.title: Your answer
steps: Add the candidates you consider equivalent, best first. Move one, remove one and use Undo.
Try “Keep initial order”, then make a partial ranking of one to four candidates and check it.
Try “None of these” and “Insufficient information”: they are different answers. An empty answer is never submitted.
This source keeps its qualifiers: a closed lid, only round pieces, at least two pieces. A broader or narrower candidate is not the same meaning.

lessons.title: The block without explanations, and your methods
steps: In one block of cases the study shows only names, IRIs and scores. You can inspect the ontologies in any way you like, or not at all.
Copy an IRI, and open “Ontology files” to find the two downloads. Downloading is optional.
After each case you will say which outside methods, if any, you used for it. Practise one report with two methods and one report with No.

requirements.label: Practise a report with two or more methods

assessment.title: Matching scores
assessment.prompt: A candidate is first in the initial order and has the highest matching score. What does this tell you?

options.label: The matcher suggests it; I should inspect the evidence.
The score is necessarily a probability of being correct.

assessment.title: Same meaning?
assessment.prompt: In a practice ontology, the source means red circles. The candidate means circles of any colour and explicitly includes blue circles. Are these the same concept?

assessment.title: Three kinds of answer
assessment.prompt: Match each situation to the answer it describes.

rows.label: You judged that none of the displayed candidates is equivalent.
You cannot make a justified judgment.
You have not chosen or submitted an answer.

assessment.title: Where information comes from
assessment.prompt: Match each kind of information to its origin.

rows.label: A feature selected or projected by Exact

part_b.prompt: The candidate has no definition in the loaded scope. Does that alone establish a contradiction with the source?

assessment.title: Outside inspection
assessment.prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: Inspecting the ontologies outside the study pages is optional.
I may combine methods and change them between cases.
After each source-and-candidates case, I report the methods I actually used.
I must keep one method for the whole study.

candidates.label: crate with a round piece
candidates.score_meaning: Illustrative practice score. In scored cases a matching score is the matcher's suggestion, never a probability of being correct.

candidates.label: closed round-piece collection crate

candidates.score_meaning: Illustrative practice score. In scored cases a matching score is the matcher's suggestion, never a probability of being correct.

candidates.label: open round-piece crate
candidates.score_meaning: Illustrative practice score. In scored cases a matching score is the matcher's suggestion, never a probability of being correct.

score_meaning.correct_feedback: Right. The initial position and the matching score are recorded advice from the matcher. Neither proves equivalence, and the score is not a calibrated probability.
score_meaning.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. A first-place, high-scoring candidate can still be wrong, and the score is not a probability of being correct. Treat it as a suggestion and inspect the evidence.

equivalence_scope.correct_feedback: Right. Circles of any colour include red circles but also blue ones, so the candidate is broader. Overlap or a broader category is not the same meaning.
equivalence_scope.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Compare the two definitions: the candidate also covers blue circles, so it is broader than the source. A broader or overlapping concept is related, but it is not equivalent.

response_states.correct_feedback: Right. None of these is an explicit judgment, Insufficient information says you cannot judge, and an empty draft is not a submitted answer.
response_states.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. None of these is a judgment that no candidate is equivalent. Insufficient information means you cannot make a justified judgment. An empty draft has not been answered or submitted at all.

evidence_origin.correct_feedback: Right. Each kind of information keeps its origin, and information missing from the loaded scope does not prove incompatibility.
evidence_origin.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Statements in the ontology are original facts, features Exact selected are matcher evidence, and prepared summaries are generated text that cites original facts. A missing, filtered or unprepared definition is not a contradiction.

external_methods.correct_feedback: Right. Outside inspection is optional, you can combine and change methods, and you report what you actually used after each case.
external_methods.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. No tool is required, and you can change methods from case to case. After each case you report the methods you actually used for that source and its candidates, not for each candidate separately.
